extracted.intended_audience: general public, cognitive scientists/psychology researchers, and stand-up comedians interested in the cognitive basis of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance summarizing cognitive constraints on what makes jokes funny, especially how mentalizing (levels of intentionality), number of characters, and complexity affect perceived humor; aimed at explaining which joke features predict funniness. Based on an empirical study of stand-up-style jokes and audience ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentalizing complexity limit
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a cognitive limit to how many nested levels of intentionality (mentalizing) people can follow in a joke; adults can comprehend up to five such levels before losing the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing mentalizing complexity improves perceived quality only up to a certain point; beyond that point people easily lose the plot and the joke is no longer funny. Conversations that share facts normally involve only three such levels, so exceeding typical audience mentalizing capacity reduces funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal number of characters / back-and-forth levels
rubrics_metrics.description: The funniest jokes involve two characters and up to five back-and-forth levels of intentionality between comedian and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding is based on analysis of 65 jokes rated by 55 undergraduates; professional comedians' successful material often conforms to this pattern. Jokes exceeding these character/intentionality bounds were rated less funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline must update expectations (unexpectedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best jokes build on a set of expectations and have a punchline that updates the listener's knowledge in an unexpected way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The punchline should change the listener's model of the situation; however, when expectations involve other people's thoughts or intentions, they become harder for the audience to track, raising cognitive demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on third-party mindstates
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations that involve the thoughts or intentions of people other than the joke-teller or audience (e.g., characters in the joke) are harder to pin down and make the joke more complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because tracking multiple other agents' mental states increases cognitive load, such jokes are more likely to exceed audience mentalizing limits and therefore be judged less funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual/observational jokes are less demanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual one-liners or undemanding observations about the world tend to involve fewer intentionality levels and are easier for audiences to process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study, about a third of jokes were factual and reasonably undemanding; these forms may be more robust in everyday conversational contexts where high mentalizing is not expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic objective: elicit laughs quickly and directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional comedians' task is to elicit laughs as directly and as fast as possible by keeping material within the mental competence of typical audience members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comics generally avoid overly intricate jokes that risk leaving the audience feeling they missed the punchline; speed and directness favor lower cognitive demand and clearer expectation–punchline structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length vs. complexity trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer, more complex jokes (multiple nested mind-twists) are more likely to exceed audience processing limits compared to one-liners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study materials included both one-liners and longer jokes; comedians must balance craft/cleverness against the increased risk that audience members will lose the plot as jokes get longer or add more intentionality layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical rating procedure (practical evaluation metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes can be evaluated on a simple numerical scale for perceived funniness (study used a four-point scale: 1 = not at all funny to 4 = very funny).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the reported study, 55 undergraduates rated 65 jokes drawn from an online 'funniest jokes' compilation; such rating scales and controlled samples can operationalize assessments of joke funniness and complexity effects.
